idiom_name: Validator.TryValidateObject / IValidatableObject.Validate called on demand, plus System.Lazy<T>
implementation_notes: The framework owns the rules but not the timing: attributes and IValidatableObject describe what is valid, and the application decides when to ask - Validator.TryValidateObject(obj, context, results, validateAllProperties: true) is the deferred gate, invoked by the operation that uses the object, and the results collection is the accumulator that replaces per-setter exceptions. System.Lazy<T> supplies the other half - deferring one expensive computation or check to first use - with LazyThreadSafetyMode choosing execution-and-publication versus publication-only semantics. Note that EF Core no longer runs data annotations or IValidatableObject during SaveChanges, so a domain-level gate must be called explicitly (in the operation or in an overridden SaveChanges) rather than trusted to the persistence layer. A hand-written validator tree is still justified when one rule set must serve both DTOs and domain types and be composed by name.
pitfalls: TryValidateObject walks only members carrying validation attributes and invokes IValidatableObject only when validateAllProperties is true, so the default overload can return an empty violation list for an object that is not valid.
Validation attributes on an entity are not run by EF Core on SaveChanges any more, so a gate that only relies on the persistence layer performs no validation at all.
Lazy<T> caches a thrown exception: a deferred check that fails once keeps failing on every later access, so checks that can succeed later must run outside the Lazy.
